source.title: Just Interpolate: Kernel "Ridgeless" Regression Can Generalize

page_placements.theme: Interpolation risk depends on signal, geometry and estimator

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no material text problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether minimum-norm kernel interpolation can generalize on natural MNIST labels, using regression rather than neural networks and without random-label controls.
record.gate_note: The study reports that interpolation has the best out-of-sample performance on all 45 digit-pair experiments on a coarse regularization grid, and in all but one pair on a finer grid. It also reports spectral-decay and synthetic-data results. The digit-pair table is too large to extract row by row under the 60-row limit; aggregate results stated in text are recorded below. Theoretical bounds and cited findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes minimum-norm kernel regression, not neural networks. Its regularization comparisons and covariance-spectrum experiments do not test any of V1–V8. Connections to neural networks are explicitly left for future work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify implicit regularization of minimum-norm kernel interpolation through high dimensionality, nonlinear kernel curvature, and favorable data geometry, under technical assumptions. MNIST supplies empirical evidence, while synthetic experiments illustrate the spectral bias–variance trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: Kernel minimum-norm regression with Gaussian/RBF kernels, not neural networks; the MNIST experiments compare regularization levels, and the synthetic experiments vary covariance spectral decay.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported generalization error changes with covariance spectral decay; the authors describe an intermediate “sweet spot.” On MNIST, interpolation is best on all 45 digit pairs on the coarse grid and all but one on the finer grid.

fits_no_version.finding: Gaussian-kernel interpolation has the lowest normalized test squared error for all 45 MNIST digit pairs on the coarse regularization grid and 44 of 45 on the finer grid.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm kernel interpolation can outperform positively regularized kernel regression on natural image-label regression tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST kernel and covariance matrices exhibit rapid eigenvalue decay; synthetic experiments show best prediction performance at an intermediate covariance spectral decay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization of ridgeless kernel regression depends on data geometry, with spectral decay controlling a bias–variance trade-off.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors describe a spherical-Gaussian theoretical example with large variance and poor interpolation performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel interpolation need not generalize well when the data lack favorable spectral structure.

record.problems: The MNIST result concerns binary regression on digit pairs, not multiclass classification; no random-label comparison is reported. The finer-grid text does not identify the one pair where interpolation was not best. Synthetic spectral-decay experiments do not establish behavior for neural networks.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C reports individual results for 45 digit pairs at λ = 0, 0.1, and 1; those 135 condition-specific values are omitted because the 60-row limit is exceeded by extracting them separately. The text's aggregate result is retained as R1. Figure 4 gives finer-grid results by pair, but the supplied text does not state which pair is the exception; the aggregate textual result is retained as R2. Figures 2, 3 and 8 show additional synthetic settings and high-noise conditions; precise figure-only values are not extracted.

untested.parts: Neural-network fitting of fixed random labels, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as neural-network width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers and tuning-dependent held-out performance.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbations, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because none measures a listed version. This does not negate the kernel-regression findings. The study is not an original source for any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Neural networks, random-label fitting and test performance, and comparisons against chance.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.

rows.subject: Kernel Ridge Regression with Gaussian kernel
rows.operation_detail: Compared out-of-sample error for λ = 0, 0.1, and 1 on each of 45 distinct MNIST digit pairs; the text reports the aggregate comparison.
rows.measure: Out-of-sample prediction error, normalized by the test-set label variance
rows.value: Among all 45 experiments, no-regularization performs the best.
rows.note: Aggregate result over 45 separately reported digit-pair experiments; individual table values are omitted due to the row limit.
rows.check: The reported comparison is accurate: zero regularization gives the lowest normalized test squared error for all 45 digit pairs. Kernel regression without random-label controls does not measure V1, and changing regularization does not measure network width in V2.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1, equation (6.1) and first experiment; Appendix C.

rows.subject: Kernel Ridge Regression with Gaussian kernel

rows.measure: Out-of-sample prediction error, normalized by the test-set label variance
rows.baseline: positive λ values in the stated grid
rows.value: In all but one pair, the interpolation estimator performs the best in out-of-sample prediction.
rows.note: Aggregate result over 45 digit-pair experiments; the text does not identify the exception.
rows.check: The finer-grid aggregate is accurate, but its one exception does not constitute partial evidence for any listed version. No neural networks or width sweeps are tested.

rows.subject: Minimum-norm interpolating estimator
rows.operation_detail: Examined empirical kernel-matrix and sample-covariance eigenvalue decay on MNIST digit pairs.
rows.value: Both plots exhibit a fast decay of eigenvalues.
rows.note: The authors present this as supporting the theoretical finding that interpolation performs well in such situations.
rows.check: The measured subjects are empirical kernel and covariance matrices. Their eigenvalue decay is a descriptive property, not a direct measurement of any listed effect.

rows.subject: Minimum-norm interpolating estimator
rows.operation_detail: Described a spherical-Gaussian design where the variance term itself is large in the high-dimensional regime.
rows.value: The variance term itself is large; good L2μ convergence cannot be established.
rows.note: The paper describes this as an example where interpolation performs poorly.
rows.check: This is a theoretical example discussed in Section 6.1, not a reported empirical measurement. Large variance and failure of good L2 convergence concern kernel interpolation and should not be recorded as an absent neural-network effect.
